subject: chemistry
title: S1.5 Ideal gases
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: S1.5 Ideal gases — IB Diploma Programme Chemistry (guide first assessment 2025), topic S1.5.
meta_desc: IB DP Chemistry practice covering S1.5 Ideal gases, guide topic S1.5.
final_note: You worked through S1.5 Ideal gases — 4 guide statements.

concepts.def: A model gas whose particles are in constant random motion, have negligible volume compared with the volume of the gas, exert no intermolecular forces on one another, and collide elastically. An ideal gas would obey PV = nRT exactly at every temperature and pressure.

A collision in which the total kinetic energy of the colliding particles is the same after the collision as before: kinetic energy may be transferred from one particle to another, but none is lost. Because all collisions in the ideal gas model are elastic, a gas kept at constant temperature does not 'run down'.

The force per unit area exerted by a gas on the walls of its container; SI unit the pascal, Pa (1 Pa = 1 N m⁻²). In the particle model it arises from the collisions of the moving particles with the walls, so it acts equally in all directions.

An actual gas, whose particles have a finite volume and exert intermolecular forces on one another. Real gases behave almost ideally at high temperature and low pressure and deviate from the ideal gas model, particularly at low temperature and high pressure.

concepts.term: Limitations of the ideal gas model
concepts.def: At high pressure the particles are close together, so their own volume is no longer negligible compared with the volume of the gas and the attractions between them become significant. At low temperature the particles move more slowly, so intermolecular attractions have a greater effect on their motion. A gas with strong intermolecular forces (e.g. hydrogen-bonded NH₃) deviates more than one with very weak forces (e.g. He). The explanation is qualitative only.

concepts.term: Molar volume of a gas, V_m
concepts.def: The volume occupied by one mole of a gas at a stated temperature and pressure; unit dm³ mol⁻¹ (or m³ mol⁻¹). For an ideal gas it is the same for every gas at a given temperature and pressure, because the volume depends only on the number of particles. At STP it is 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹. V = n × V_m.
273 K (0 °C) and 100 kPa (1.00 × 10⁵ Pa): the conditions at which the molar volume of an ideal gas is 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹.

Temperature on the kelvin scale: T/K = t/°C + 273. Zero kelvin (−273 °C) is absolute zero. The gas relationships, PV = nRT and the combined gas law all use absolute temperature, never Celsius temperature.

p is inversely proportional to V, so pV is constant: halving V doubles p. A graph of p against V is a curve that falls ever less steeply; a graph of p against 1/V is a straight line through the origin.

V is directly proportional to absolute temperature, so V/T is constant. A graph of V against T in kelvin is a straight line through the origin; a graph of V against temperature in °C is a straight line that, extended, meets the temperature axis at −273 °C.

p is directly proportional to absolute temperature, so p/T is constant. A graph of p against T in kelvin is a straight line through the origin; against temperature in °C, the extended line meets the temperature axis at −273 °C.

PV = nRT, where P is the pressure in Pa, V the volume in m³, n the amount of gas in mol, R the gas constant and T the absolute temperature in K. Pressure and volume must be in SI units: 1 kPa = 10³ Pa, 1 dm³ = 10⁻³ m³, 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³.
R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. With P in Pa and V in m³ the product PV is in joules (Pa m³ = N m⁻² × m³ = N m = J), which is why R carries the unit J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ for a fixed amount of an ideal gas whose pressure, volume and temperature change from state 1 to state 2. It follows from PV = nRT with n constant. Temperatures must be in kelvin, and pressure and volume must be in the same units on both sides.

mcqs.q: Which statement is one of the key assumptions of the ideal gas model?
options: The particles lose a small amount of kinetic energy in every collision.
The spaces between the particles are filled with air that separates them.
The particles repel one another, which keeps them spread through the container.
The particles have a negligible volume compared with the volume of the gas.
mcqs.specStatementText: An ideal gas consists of moving particles with negligible volume and no intermolecular forces. All collisions between particles are considered elastic.
mcqs.explain: This is one of the model's assumptions: the particles are treated as having no volume of their own compared with the space the gas occupies. The other key assumptions are that the particles are moving, exert no intermolecular forces, and collide elastically.
rationales: A student who thinks moving particles must gradually run down picks this. The model assumes that all collisions are elastic: kinetic energy passes between particles in a collision but the total is not lost, so a gas at constant temperature does not slow down.

A student who cannot accept empty space between particles picks this. In the model the space between the particles is empty. Air is itself a gas made of particles, so it cannot fill the gaps between gas particles.

A student who pictures gas particles pushing each other apart picks this. The model assumes there are no intermolecular forces at all, attractive or repulsive; the gas spreads through the container because its particles move randomly.

This is one of the model's assumptions: the particles are treated as having no volume of their own compared with the space the gas occupies. The other key assumptions are that the particles are moving, exert no intermolecular forces, and collide elastically.

mcqs.q: According to the ideal gas model, what causes the pressure that a gas exerts on the walls of its container?
options: Moving particles collide with the walls and exert a force on them.
The particles repel one another, so they push outwards on the walls.
The weight of the particles presses on the container, mainly on its base.
The particles expand to fill the container and press against its walls.
mcqs.specStatementText: An ideal gas consists of moving particles with negligible volume and no intermolecular forces. All collisions between particles are considered elastic.
mcqs.explain: In the model the particles move randomly and collide elastically with the walls. Each collision exerts a force on the wall; the pressure is the total force per unit area from these collisions, so it acts equally on every wall.
rationales: In the model the particles move randomly and collide elastically with the walls. Each collision exerts a force on the wall; the pressure is the total force per unit area from these collisions, so it acts equally on every wall.

A student who pictures gas particles pushing each other apart picks this. The ideal gas model has no intermolecular forces, attractive or repulsive; the pressure comes from particles colliding with the walls as they move.

A student who links pressure to weight, as for a solid resting on a surface, picks this. Gas pressure acts equally in all directions, including upwards on a lid; it comes from particle collisions with the walls, not from the weight of the gas.

A student who gives the particles the properties of the bulk gas picks this. Particles do not change size; a gas fills its container because its particles move freely through the empty space, and the pressure comes from their collisions with the walls.

mcqs.q: A sample of nitrogen is held at a pressure of 2.0 × 10⁶ Pa, first at 150 K and then at 600 K. It is a gas at both temperatures. At which temperature does it deviate more from ideal gas behaviour, and why?
options: At 150 K, as its particles have stopped moving and so no longer collide
At 150 K, as its slower particles are affected more by the attractions between them
At 600 K, as its faster particles collide more violently with each other
At 600 K, as its particles expand when heated and take up more space
mcqs.specStatementText: Real gases deviate from the ideal gas model, particularly at low temperature and high pressure.
mcqs.explain: At low temperature the particles have less kinetic energy, so the intermolecular attractions, which the ideal model ignores, have a significant effect on their motion. Real gases deviate most at low temperature and high pressure.
rationales: A student who believes particles stop moving when cold picks this. The particles of a gas are always moving: at 150 K nitrogen is still a gas and exerts a pressure because its particles collide with the walls. They move more slowly, which is why the attractions between them matter more.

At low temperature the particles have less kinetic energy, so the intermolecular attractions, which the ideal model ignores, have a significant effect on their motion. Real gases deviate most at low temperature and high pressure.

A student who thinks fast, energetic particles break the model picks this. A real gas behaves more ideally at high temperature, because the particles' kinetic energy is then large compared with the attractions between them. Deviation is greatest at low temperature.

A student who thinks particles swell when heated picks this. Particles do not change size with temperature. At 600 K and the same pressure the gas occupies a larger volume and its particles move faster, so it behaves more ideally, not less.

mcqs.q: Four gases are each at 300 K and 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Which gas deviates most from ideal gas behaviour?
options: Helium, He, as its light atoms move the fastest and collide most violently
Neon, Ne, as its atoms are the heaviest and so they occupy the most space
Ammonia, NH₃, as hydrogen bonding attracts its molecules to one another
Methane, CH₄, as each molecule is held together by four C–H bonds
mcqs.specStatementText: Real gases deviate from the ideal gas model, particularly at low temperature and high pressure.
mcqs.explain: Ammonia molecules form hydrogen bonds with one another, so the attractions between them are much stronger than between the particles of the other three gases. The ideal gas model assumes no intermolecular forces, so the gas with the strongest attractions deviates most.
rationales: A student who thinks high particle speed makes a gas less ideal picks this. Helium is one of the most nearly ideal gases: its atoms are small and the London forces between them are extremely weak. Fast particles are less affected by attractions, not more.

A student who equates a heavier particle with a larger one, and thinks size decides the deviation, picks this. Neon atoms (M = 20.18 g mol⁻¹) are heavier than ammonia molecules (17.04 g mol⁻¹), but the London forces between them are weak, so neon behaves almost ideally. The strength of the attractions between particles decides the deviation, not their mass.

Ammonia molecules form hydrogen bonds with one another, so the attractions between them are much stronger than between the particles of the other three gases. The ideal gas model assumes no intermolecular forces, so the gas with the strongest attractions deviates most.

A student who counts the covalent bonds inside a molecule as the forces between molecules picks this. The four C–H bonds hold each methane molecule together but do not attract one methane molecule to another. Methane molecules attract one another only by London forces, which are much weaker than the hydrogen bonding between ammonia molecules.

mcqs.q: At STP (273 K, 100 kPa), 1.00 mol of helium (M = 4.00 g mol⁻¹) occupies 22.7 dm³. What volume does 1.00 mol of xenon (M = 131.29 g mol⁻¹) occupy at STP, if both behave as ideal gases?
options: 22.7 dm³, as heavy xenon atoms move at the same speed as the helium atoms
22.7 dm³, as volume depends only on the amount of gas at a given T and p
More than 22.7 dm³, as its much larger atoms take up more of the space
Less than 22.7 dm³, as a denser gas has its particles closer together
mcqs.specStatementText: The molar volume of an ideal gas is a constant at a specific temperature and pressure.
mcqs.explain: In an ideal gas the particles have negligible volume and exert no intermolecular forces, so at a given temperature and pressure the volume depends only on the amount of gas, not on the identity or mass of the particles. 1.00 mol of xenon at STP occupies the same 22.7 dm³ as 1.00 mol of helium.
mcqs.working: Both samples are at the same temperature (273 K) and pressure (100 kPa) and contain the same amount of gas (1.00 mol). For an ideal gas V = nRT/p, which does not contain the molar mass, so V(Xe) = V(He) = 1.00 mol × 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ = 22.7 dm³.
rationales: A student who thinks all particles move at the same speed at a given temperature picks this. At the same temperature the particles have the same average kinetic energy, so the heavier xenon atoms move much more slowly than helium atoms. The xenon sample occupies 22.7 dm³ because volume depends only on the amount of gas, not because the speeds are equal.

In an ideal gas the particles have negligible volume and exert no intermolecular forces, so at a given temperature and pressure the volume depends only on the amount of gas, not on the identity or mass of the particles. 1.00 mol of xenon at STP occupies the same 22.7 dm³ as 1.00 mol of helium.

A student who thinks bigger or heavier particles need more room picks this. The particles' own volume is negligible compared with the volume of the gas, so the size of the xenon atoms does not affect the molar volume: 1.00 mol of xenon occupies 22.7 dm³, the same as 1.00 mol of helium.

A student who explains density by particle spacing picks this: xenon is far denser than helium, so its atoms seem to be packed more closely. At the same temperature and pressure equal amounts of ideal gases occupy equal volumes, so the spacing is the same; xenon is denser because each of its atoms has a much larger mass.

mcqs.q: What volume does 72.0 g of oxygen gas, O₂, occupy at STP (273 K, 100 kPa)? Molar volume of an ideal gas at STP = 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹; A_r(O) = 16.00.
mcqs.specStatementText: The molar volume of an ideal gas is a constant at a specific temperature and pressure.
rationales: A student who uses 16.00 g mol⁻¹, the molar mass of oxygen atoms, gets n = 72.0 ÷ 16.00 = 4.50 mol and V = 4.50 × 22.7 = 102 dm³. Oxygen gas consists of O₂ molecules, so M = 32.00 g mol⁻¹.
A student who multiplies the mass by the molar volume gets 72.0 × 22.7 = 1634 dm³. The molar volume is the volume per mole, so the mass must first be converted to amount: n = 72.0 ÷ 32.00 = 2.25 mol.
A student who divides the molar volume by the amount gets 22.7 ÷ 2.25 = 10.1 dm³. The volume is the amount multiplied by the volume per mole: V = n × V_m = 2.25 × 22.7 = 51.1 dm³.

mcqs.q: A fixed mass of an ideal gas is kept at constant pressure. Its volume is measured at several temperatures and plotted against temperature in °C. Which description of the graph is correct?
options: A straight line meeting the axis at −273 °C, where volume would be zero
A straight line meeting the axis at −273 °C, where the particles shrink to nothing
A straight line through the origin, since volume is proportional to temperature in °C
A horizontal line, as the gas fills the same container at every temperature
mcqs.specStatementText: The molar volume of an ideal gas is a constant at a specific temperature and pressure.
mcqs.explain: Volume is proportional to absolute temperature. On a Celsius axis the line does not pass through the origin; extended backwards, it reaches zero volume at −273 °C (0 K), absolute zero. (A real gas would liquefy before this; the line is an extrapolation.)
rationales: Volume is proportional to absolute temperature. On a Celsius axis the line does not pass through the origin; extended backwards, it reaches zero volume at −273 °C (0 K), absolute zero. (A real gas would liquefy before this; the line is an extrapolation.)

A student who thinks particles shrink as they cool picks this. The intercept is right but the reason is not: particles do not change size. The volume falls because slower particles hit the walls less hard and less often, so at constant pressure the gas occupies less space.

A student who treats 0 °C as zero temperature picks this. 0 °C is only the melting point of ice, and a gas at 0 °C still has a large volume. Volume is proportional to temperature in kelvin, so on a Celsius axis the line meets the axis at −273 °C.

A student who thinks a gas always has the volume of its container picks this. A gas does fill its container, but at constant pressure the container (for example a gas syringe) expands as the gas is heated, so the volume increases steadily with temperature.

mcqs.q: For a fixed mass of an ideal gas at constant temperature, the pressure, p, is plotted on the y-axis against 1/V on the x-axis, where V is the volume. Which description of the graph is correct?
options: A straight line with a negative gradient, as p falls as 1/V rises
A curve that falls and levels off, as p and V are inversely related
A straight line through the origin, as p doubles whenever V is halved
A horizontal line, as the particles' speed and hence p do not change
mcqs.specStatementText: The molar volume of an ideal gas is a constant at a specific temperature and pressure.
mcqs.explain: At constant temperature p is inversely proportional to V, so p is directly proportional to 1/V: halving V doubles 1/V and doubles p. A graph of p against 1/V is therefore a straight line through the origin.
rationales: A student who thinks an inverse relationship is always a falling straight line picks this. p is inversely proportional to V, so p is directly proportional to 1/V: as 1/V rises p rises, giving a straight line through the origin with a positive gradient.

A student who expects every inverse relationship to look like a falling curve picks this without reading the x-axis. The falling curve is the graph of p against V. Plotting against 1/V turns the inverse relationship into a direct one: a straight line through the origin.

At constant temperature p is inversely proportional to V, so p is directly proportional to 1/V: halving V doubles 1/V and doubles p. A graph of p against 1/V is therefore a straight line through the origin.

A student who thinks pressure depends only on how fast the particles move picks this. At constant temperature the average speed is unchanged, but in a smaller volume the particles hit the walls more often, so the pressure rises as V falls.

mcqs.q: A fixed mass of an ideal gas in a gas syringe is heated at constant pressure from 20 °C to 40 °C. What happens to its volume?
options: It rises by about 7%, since its temperature in K does
It doubles, since 20 °C to 40 °C doubles its temperature
It increases, since each gas particle expands when heated
It stays the same, since the gas still fills the same syringe
mcqs.specStatementText: The molar volume of an ideal gas is a constant at a specific temperature and pressure.
mcqs.explain: At constant pressure V is proportional to absolute temperature. 20 °C = 293 K and 40 °C = 313 K, so V₂/V₁ = 313/293 = 1.07: the absolute temperature and the volume both rise by about 7%.
rationales: At constant pressure V is proportional to absolute temperature. 20 °C = 293 K and 40 °C = 313 K, so V₂/V₁ = 313/293 = 1.07: the absolute temperature and the volume both rise by about 7%.

A student who treats Celsius temperature as proportional to volume picks this. 0 °C is not absolute zero, so doubling the Celsius temperature does not double the absolute temperature: 293 K to 313 K is a rise of only about 7%.

A student who thinks particles swell when heated picks this. The volume does increase, but not because the particles grow: they move faster, so to keep the pressure constant the gas must occupy more space. The increase is a factor of 313/293.
A student who thinks a gas always has the volume of its container picks this. The plunger of a gas syringe moves, so at constant pressure the gas expands as it is heated: V₂/V₁ = 313/293.

mcqs.q: What volume is occupied by 0.0472 mol of an ideal gas at 30 °C and 125 kPa? R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
mcqs.specStatementText: The relationship between the pressure, volume, temperature and amount of an ideal gas is shown in the ideal gas equation PV = nRT and the combined gas law P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.
rationales: A student who leaves the temperature in °C gets 0.0472 × 8.31 × 30 ÷ (1.25 × 10⁵) = 9.41 × 10⁻⁵ m³. PV = nRT needs absolute temperature: 30 °C = 303 K.
A student who substitutes the pressure in kPa gets 0.0472 × 8.31 × 303 ÷ 125 = 0.951 m³, 1000 times too large. With R in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ the pressure must be in Pa: 125 kPa = 1.25 × 10⁵ Pa.
A student who uses the molar volume at STP gets 0.0472 mol × 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ = 1.07 dm³ = 1.07 × 10⁻³ m³. 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ applies only at 273 K and 100 kPa; at 303 K and 125 kPa use PV = nRT.

mcqs.q: A gas syringe contains 2.20 cm³ of an ideal gas at 20 °C and 1.20 × 10⁵ Pa. What amount of gas does it contain? R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
mcqs.specStatementText: The relationship between the pressure, volume, temperature and amount of an ideal gas is shown in the ideal gas equation PV = nRT and the combined gas law P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.
rationales: A student who leaves the temperature in °C gets 0.264 ÷ (8.31 × 20) = 1.59 × 10⁻³ mol. PV = nRT needs absolute temperature: 20 °C = 293 K.
A student who converts cm³ to m³ by dividing by 1000, as for dm³, uses V = 2.20 × 10⁻³ m³ and gets 0.108 mol, 1000 times too large. 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³, so 2.20 cm³ = 2.20 × 10⁻⁶ m³.
A student who uses the molar volume at STP gets 2.20 × 10⁻³ dm³ ÷ 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ = 9.69 × 10⁻⁵ mol. 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ applies only at 273 K and 100 kPa; at 293 K and 1.20 × 10⁵ Pa use PV = nRT.

mcqs.q: A fixed mass of an ideal gas occupies 2.00 × 10⁻³ m³ at 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa and 27 °C. It is compressed to 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³ and at the same time its temperature rises to 87 °C. What is its new pressure?
mcqs.specStatementText: The relationship between the pressure, volume, temperature and amount of an ideal gas is shown in the ideal gas equation PV = nRT and the combined gas law P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.
mcqs.explain: T₁ = 300 K and T₂ = 360 K. P₂ = P₁ × (V₁/V₂) × (T₂/T₁) = 1.00 × 10⁵ × 4.00 × 1.20 = 4.80 × 10⁵ Pa. The compression and the heating both raise the pressure.
rationales: A student who uses the Celsius temperatures gets 1.00 × 10⁵ × 4.00 × 87/27 = 1.29 × 10⁶ Pa. The combined gas law needs absolute temperatures: 300 K and 360 K.
A student who inverts the temperature ratio gets 1.00 × 10⁵ × 4.00 × 300/360 = 3.33 × 10⁵ Pa, as if heating lowered the pressure. From P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂, P₂ = P₁ × (V₁/V₂) × (T₂/T₁).
T₁ = 300 K and T₂ = 360 K. P₂ = P₁ × (V₁/V₂) × (T₂/T₁) = 1.00 × 10⁵ × 4.00 × 1.20 = 4.80 × 10⁵ Pa. The compression and the heating both raise the pressure.

A student who applies only the pressure–volume relationship gets 1.00 × 10⁵ × 4.00 = 4.00 × 10⁵ Pa, ignoring the rise in temperature. Both variables changed, so the factor T₂/T₁ = 360/300 must be included.

mcqs.q: A sample of methane, CH₄, is kept at 300 K, first at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and then at 2.0 × 10⁷ Pa. It is a gas at both pressures. At which pressure does it deviate more from ideal gas behaviour, and why?
options: At 2.0 × 10⁷ Pa, as its particles collide more often and lose kinetic energy each time
At 2.0 × 10⁷ Pa, as its particles are close enough for their volume and attractions to matter
At 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, as its particles expand to fill the much larger volume of the gas
Neither, as at 300 K its particles move at the same average speed at both pressures
mcqs.specStatementText: Real gases deviate from the ideal gas model, particularly at low temperature and high pressure.
mcqs.explain: At high pressure the particles are close together, so their own volume is no longer negligible compared with the volume of the gas, and the attractions between them become significant. The ideal gas model ignores both, so methane deviates more at 2.0 × 10⁷ Pa. Real gases deviate most at low temperature and high pressure.
rationales: A student who thinks every collision loses kinetic energy picks this. Collisions are elastic in the model and, for a real gas at 300 K, the average kinetic energy of the particles is set by the temperature, which is the same at both pressures. The deviation at high pressure comes from the particles' own volume and the attractions between them.

At high pressure the particles are close together, so their own volume is no longer negligible compared with the volume of the gas, and the attractions between them become significant. The ideal gas model ignores both, so methane deviates more at 2.0 × 10⁷ Pa. Real gases deviate most at low temperature and high pressure.

A student who thinks particles swell to fill their container picks this. Particles do not change size. At low pressure the particles are far apart, so their volume and the attractions between them are negligible and the gas behaves almost ideally.

A student who thinks deviation depends only on how fast the particles move (and so only on temperature) picks this. The average speed is indeed the same at both pressures, but at 2.0 × 10⁷ Pa the particles are much closer together, so their own volume and the attractions between them become significant.

mcqs.q: The graph shows PV / nRT plotted against pressure for a real gas at constant temperature, together with the line for an ideal gas. Which statement explains the behaviour of the real gas at the point marked A?
options: Attractions between the molecules pull them closer together, so the gas occupies a smaller volume than an ideal gas would.
The covalent bonds within each molecule are strong, and these bonds hold the neighbouring molecules close together.
The molecules have a volume of their own, so the gas is squeezed into less space than the ideal model predicts.
The molecules lose kinetic energy in their frequent collisions, so they strike the walls with less force than ideal particles.
mcqs.specStatementText: Real gases deviate from the ideal gas model, particularly at low temperature and high pressure.
mcqs.explain: The ideal model assumes no intermolecular forces. In a real gas the attractions between molecules reduce the volume (or the pressure on the walls) below the ideal value, so PV/nRT < 1 at A. At higher pressure (B) the molecules’ own volume dominates and the curve rises above the line.
rationales: The ideal model assumes no intermolecular forces. In a real gas the attractions between molecules reduce the volume (or the pressure on the walls) below the ideal value, so PV/nRT < 1 at A. At higher pressure (B) the molecules’ own volume dominates and the curve rises above the line.

Covalent bonds act within a molecule and have no effect on how molecules attract one another. The dip at A is caused by the intermolecular attractions (van der Waals forces) between molecules, which the ideal model ignores.

The molecules’ own volume acts the other way: it makes the gas harder to compress, so PV/nRT rises above 1 (the region around B). The dip at A comes from the attractions between molecules, which draw them closer together.

Collisions do not drain kinetic energy from a gas; at constant temperature the average kinetic energy is unchanged. The lower value of PV/nRT at A is due to attractions between the molecules, not to slower molecules.

mcqs.q: The graph shows the volume of a fixed mass of an ideal gas at constant pressure plotted against temperature in °C. Measurements were made between 27 °C and 227 °C and the line is extrapolated back to the temperature axis. At what temperature would the volume of the gas be 48.0 cm³?
mcqs.specStatementText: The molar volume of an ideal gas is a constant at a specific temperature and pressure.
mcqs.explain: The line reaches zero volume at −273 °C, so V is proportional to the kelvin temperature. V = 40.0 cm³ at 227 °C (500 K), so V = 48.0 cm³ at 500 × 48.0/40.0 = 600 K, which is 600 − 273 = 327 °C.
mcqs.working: From the graph, V = 40.0 cm³ at 227 °C and the line extrapolates to V = 0 at −273 °C, so V ∝ T/K. T₁ = 227 + 273 = 500 K. T₂ = T₁ × V₂/V₁ = 500 K × 48.0/40.0 = 600 K; t₂ = 600 − 273 = 327 °C.
rationales: 227 × 48.0/40.0 treats volume as proportional to the Celsius temperature, which would put zero volume at 0 °C. The graph shows zero volume at −273 °C, so work in kelvin: 500 K × 48.0/40.0 = 600 K = 327 °C.

500 × 40.0/48.0 = 417 K puts the volume ratio the wrong way round, giving a lower temperature for a larger volume. The graph shows volume rising with temperature: T = 500 K × 48.0/40.0 = 600 K = 327 °C.
The line reaches zero volume at −273 °C, so V is proportional to the kelvin temperature. V = 40.0 cm³ at 227 °C (500 K), so V = 48.0 cm³ at 500 × 48.0/40.0 = 600 K, which is 600 − 273 = 327 °C.
600 is the temperature in kelvin. The question asks in °C, so subtract 273: 600 K = 327 °C.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Chemistry (guide first assessment 2025); topic S1.5 Ideal gases

specStatements.text: An ideal gas consists of moving particles with negligible volume and no intermolecular forces. All collisions between particles are considered elastic.
specStatements.guidance: Recognize the key assumptions in the ideal gas model.

specStatements.text: Real gases deviate from the ideal gas model, particularly at low temperature and high pressure.
specStatements.guidance: Explain the limitations of the ideal gas model. No mathematical coverage is required.

specStatements.text: The molar volume of an ideal gas is a constant at a specific temperature and pressure.
specStatements.guidance: Investigate the relationship between temperature, pressure and volume for a fixed mass of an ideal gas and analyse graphs relating these variables. The names of specific gas laws will not be assessed. The value for the molar volume of an ideal gas under standard temperature and pressure (STP) is given in the data booklet.

specStatements.text: The relationship between the pressure, volume, temperature and amount of an ideal gas is shown in the ideal gas equation PV = nRT and the combined gas law P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.
specStatements.guidance: Solve problems relating to the ideal gas equation. Units of volume and pressure should be SI only. The value of the gas constant R, the ideal gas equation, and the combined gas law, are given in the data booklet.

scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item uses a real-gas equation, a correction term or a compressibility factor. Deviations from ideal behaviour are explained only qualitatively, in terms of particle volume and intermolecular attractions.

scopeNotes.statement: The names of specific gas laws will not be assessed.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No stem, option, rationale or card names a gas law after a scientist. The relationships are stated in terms of the variables (for example 'p is inversely proportional to V at constant temperature'); only the guide's own terms 'ideal gas equation' and 'combined gas law' are used.

scopeNotes.statement: Units of volume and pressure should be SI only.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every calculation with PV = nRT or the combined gas law is worked in Pa and m³ (with R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and T in K). Where a stem quotes kPa or cm³, the working converts to SI before substituting, and failing to convert is tested as an error.
